 On the other hand, Mr. M. A. Rouf, appearing for the respondents argued that in deciding this point, the general scheme of the Act is to be taken into consideration. The general scheme of the Act is that for the purpose of taking over all interests that are liable to be acquired under the Act, preparation of record-of-rights is to be made and after final publication of the record-of-rights, assessment of compensation of the acquirable interests is to be made and finally published. It, however, seems that an exception has been made with regard to rent-receiving interests and special provisions for acquisition of the interests of certain rent-recovers have been made in Chapter II of Part 11 of the Act. According to the provisions of this Chapter, rent-receiving interests can be acquired by publication of Notification under section 3 of the Act even before the general provisions of the Act are given effect to, that is, before preparation of the record-of rights and preparation and publication of the Compensation Assessment roll. It may also be pointed out that according to the provisions of section 3 of the Act, before introduction of the sub-section (2a) M section 3 by way of amendment. Notification under section 3 was to be published with re3ference to particular estates, talks, tenures, holdings and tenancies and in respect of all rent-receivers whose properties were under the management of court of Wards Act, 1879. Sub-section (2a) was enacted and introduced in section 3 of the Act by Ordinance No.III of 1956. This provision namely, sub-section (2a) empowers the Government to publish Notification under section 3 in respect of rent-receivers by name or by reference to areas wherein they have interests or in such other manner as the Government might determine. It is after this amendment that general Notification dated 2nd April, 1956 were issued District-wise in regard to all rent-receiving interests which thereafter vested in the Government with effect from 14.4.56 in terms of those Notifications. So, Mr. Rout submitted that it was futile to argue that these interests. which were the subject-matter of the general Notifications, contained even after 14th April. 1956 and that they did not vest in the Government. His contention was that in the instant case the rent-receiving interests of the raiyat legally vested in the Government which became the proprietor by virtue of acquisition of the said interests. Accordingly from 14.4. 56 the Government alone became entitled, under the law, to receive the rent. The previous rent-receivers became divested of the right to receive rent and consequently they disappeared from the sense. This enactment has been promulgated long after all the acquisition proceedings were completed and long after the observations of the High Court made regarding the non-preparation of the compensation assessment roll. The enactment made in President's Order No. 90 of 1972 clearly states that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force. on the commencement of this Order all suits, appeals applications and other legal proceedings pending or continuing or deemed to be pending or continuing in any court against the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh in which the legality or validity of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 1950 or of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance. 1956 or of any other law making any amendment in the said Act or of the acquisition of any property made under any provision thereof is challenged or called in question shall abate, and all orders, including orders of injunction and other interlocutory orders passed in such suit, appeals applications and other legal Proceedings shall cease to have any effect; and; and no court shall entertain and no person shall bring fresh suit, appeals application or other legal proceedings in which the legality or validity of any such law or acquisition is challenged or called in question. 

 The directive in the law is therefore clear that on the costing into operation of this Order, notwithstanding any other earlier view of law on the subject, a pending proceeding or a proceeding which is sought to instituted challenging or calling in question the acquisition of any property under any of the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act shall abate and no proceedings shall be instituted in any Court.

 21. Mr. Narul Amin learned Advocate, referred to an unreported decision of the Appellate Division of the Hon'ble Supreme Court. i.e. the case of Salahudin Khan and others-Vs- Md. Abdul Hai Bahar and others, Civil Appeal No. 149 of 2008, in which, the Appellate Division of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of Bangladesh on the question of rejection of the plaint was of the opinion that: 

 "The only claim of the defendants on which they sought to dismiss the suit was that the plaintiff No. I company was not properly represented and the other plaintiffs being neither Directors of the company nor its Share-holders had right to represent the company. In the plaint. it was categorically stated that after the death of Sirajul Islam Khan, Managing Director of the company, plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3 being his son and wile became the directors of the company and as such they were entitled to redeem the mortgaged property. The plea taken by the defendants in the application that none of the said plaintiffs have got 5000/ shares to become the director of the company nor the company approved them to the Shareholders of the company are purely question of fact which shall have to be thrashed out on the basis of the evidence of the produced by the parties at the tie of hearing of the suit, particularly the suit being at the stage of peremptory hearing. Considering all statements made in the plaint as well, as in the application, it appears to as that none of the situations as contemplated in Order VII, rule 11 of the Code was attracted. It a true that the provisions of rule 11 are not exhaustive in the matter of rejection of plaint and in exceptional situation a plaint can be rejected under section 151 of the Code even if it does not come within the mischief of this rule, but such situation is absent in the instant ease. It is also a fact that the application for dismissal of the suit was filed after about 9(nine) years from the date of filing of the suit when the same was at the stage of peremptory hearing. The very filing of the application at such a belated stage particularly when the suit was fixed for peremptory hearing does not show bonafide on the part of defendants. It appears to as that the application was filed just to delay the disposal of the suit. In the above context, the learned Joint District Judge while rejecting the application lightly observed that on issue as to the maintainability having already been framed, the same shall be decided along with other issues, the learned District Judge rightly affirmed the said view of the learned Joint District Judge, but the learned Judges of the High Court Division totally failed to consider the above discussed factual and legal aspect of the case as well as observations of the Court below."
